France : les lycéens reprennent les blocages, Greta Thunberg rejoint la mobilisation
items.description: La mobilisation des lycéens et des étudiants s’est poursuivie mardi 13 octobre dans plusieurs villes françaises. Les manifestants réclament notamment la suppression de Parcoursup et un plan d’investissement de 10 milliards d’euros pour les lycées. À Saint-Denis, la militante écologiste Greta Thunberg s’est jointe au mouvement. Les rues françaises connaissent une nouvelle journée de mobilisation lycéenne et étudiante. Mardi 13 octobre, plusieurs établissements ont été bloqués à Paris, Rennes, Montpellier et Bayonne, dans le cadre de la cinquième journée d’action depuis le début du mouvement, le 17 septembre. À Saint-Denis, au nord de Paris, Greta Thunberg, militante écologiste suédoise de 23 ans, a rejoint les élèves mobilisés devant le lycée Paul-Éluard. Une vingtaine d’avocats en robe noire étaient également présents pour former une chaîne destinée à protéger les lycéens, alors que des incidents et des critiques concernant les interventions policières ont marqué les précédentes journées. À Paris, plusieurs établissements ont été bloqués dès le début de la matinée. Une manifestation était prévue à 14 heures en direction de l’esplanade des Invalides, à proximité des bureaux du Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu et du ministère de l’Éducation. Les organisations lycéennes et étudiantes réclament notamment la suppression de Parcoursup, la plateforme nationale d’orientation dans l’enseignement supérieur, ainsi qu’un plan de 10 milliards d’euros en faveur des lycées. Selon le ministre de l’Éducation français, Édouard Geffray, environ 200 lycées devaient être fermés mardi. Il évoque toutefois une baisse de la mobilisation par rapport aux semaines précédentes. Les manifestants, eux, ne comptent pas abandonner. Certains espèrent notamment que la journée de mobilisation prévue le 17 octobre contre la vie chère donnera un nouvel élan au mouvement. Face à cette mobilisation, Emmanuel Macron a appelé les manifestants à agir dans le calme et à respecter les personnes et les biens. Le dispositif policier reste important dans plusieurs villes, notamment à Bayonne, où une dizaine de fourgons de CRS étaient déployés près du lycée Louis-de-Foix dès le matin. Certains élèves dénoncent des moyens disproportionnés et une forme d’intimidation. À l’approche des vacances scolaires, le gouvernement espère un ralentissement du mouvement. Les organisations mobilisées affirment cependant vouloir poursuivre leur action jusqu’à l’obtention de réponses concrètes à leurs revendications. The post France : les lycéens reprennent les blocages, Greta Thunberg rejoint la mobilisation appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Musique guinéenne : un colloque annoncé les 22 et 23 octobre au Musée national
items.description: Le Musée national de Guinée accueillera, les 22 et 23 octobre 2026, un colloque consacré à l’histoire de la culture guinéenne, avec un accent particulier sur la musique, son évolution et sa contribution à la création d’emplois. À travers cette initiative, des professionnels du secteur entendent transmettre leur expérience aux jeunes générations et approfondir la réflexion sur les enjeux économiques et numériques de la culture. Intitulé « De l’authenticité à la digitalisation : la musique guinéenne comme vecteur d’identité et de création d’emplois », ce rendez-vous réunira des historiens, des professeurs, des hommes de culture, des artistes, des journalistes culturels, des opérateurs du secteur et des étudiants de l’Institut supérieur des arts Mory Kanté. Pour les initiateurs, l’enjeu dépasse la simple célébration du patrimoine artistique national. Il s’agit de retracer les grandes étapes de l’histoire culturelle du pays, de faire connaître des pans parfois méconnus de cette évolution et de réfléchir aux moyens de mieux valoriser les productions artistiques guinéennes. Lors de la présentation de l’initiative, l’homme de culture Fodéba Isto Keira a insisté sur la nécessité de transmettre aux jeunes les connaissances accumulées au fil de plusieurs décennies d’expérience. Selon lui, cette démarche répond à un déficit d’informations sur le parcours de la culture guinéenne et sur les personnalités qui ont contribué à son rayonnement. « L’objectif de ce colloque, c’est la transmission », a-t-il expliqué, soulignant que les organisateurs souhaitent partager leur expérience avec les nouvelles générations, notamment les étudiants et les professionnels qui évoluent dans le secteur culturel. Retracer les grandes étapes de la musique guinéenne Les échanges porteront notamment sur les origines et l’évolution de la musique guinéenne, les formations artistiques qui ont marqué son histoire, les orchestres fédéraux, les ensembles nationaux ainsi que les festivals et les initiatives qui ont contribué à son développement. Intervenant sur le thème de « L’épopée de la culture guinéenne », le journaliste culturel Jean-Baptiste Williams a estimé qu’il était nécessaire de mieux documenter cette histoire afin de la rendre accessible au grand public. Il a notamment évoqué les premières expériences théâtrales et musicales, dont certaines restent insuffisamment connues. L’intervenant a également annoncé qu’il présenterait des éléments historiques sur les premières formations musicales du pays, affirmant notamment que le premier orchestre guinéen aurait été créé en 1933. Une affirmation qui sera au cœur de la démarche de transmission historique portée par les organisateurs. De son côté, Fodéba Isto Keira a annoncé des communications consacrées à plusieurs étapes importantes de la production musicale guinéenne, notamment le rôle de la structure nationale Silyphone, qui aurait produit entre 500 et 600 références discographiques, ainsi que l’émergence des maisons de production privées. La contribution de professionnels ayant participé à cette évolution sera également mise à profit. Les discussions aborderont ainsi les métiers de la production, la conservation du patrimoine artistique et la place des acteurs qui ont accompagné l’essor de la musique guinéenne. Culture, emplois et défis du numérique Au-delà de la dimension historique, les organisateurs entendent mettre en évidence le potentiel économique de la culture. La création d’emplois, les mécanismes de production et de diffusion musicale, les droits d’auteur et la digitalisation figurent parmi les questions annoncées au programme. À l’heure où les plateformes numériques et le streaming transforment les modes de diffusion et de consommation de la musique, ces rencontres devraient permettre aux participants de mieux comprendre les possibilités offertes aux artistes et les défis auxquels ils sont confrontés. Les questions de propriété intellectuelle et de protection des œuvres seront également abordées, avec la participation de personnes ressources issues des structures concernées. L’objectif est de permettre aux professionnels, notamment aux jeunes acteurs du secteur, de mieux maîtriser les mécanismes qui encadrent la création et l’exploitation des œuvres. Pour Fodéba Isto Keira, la culture ne doit pas seulement être envisagée sous l’angle du spectacle. Elle représente également un domaine de connaissance, un patrimoine à préserver et un secteur susceptible de contribuer à l’activité économique et à l’emploi. Une démarche tournée vers la jeunesse Les organisateurs souhaitent faire de ce colloque un cadre d’apprentissage et d’échanges professionnels. Les communications seront suivies de discussions interactives et de séances de questions-réponses, afin de favoriser la participation du public et le partage d’expériences. Les initiateurs envisagent également de poursuivre cette démarche au-delà des deux journées prévues au Musée national, notamment à travers des conférences dans les universités. Destiné en priorité aux artistes, aux journalistes et animateurs culturels, aux promoteurs, aux associations professionnelles et aux cadres du ministère chargé de la Culture, le colloque se veut ouvert à toute personne intéressée par l’histoire et l’avenir du patrimoine guinéen. À travers cette rencontre, les organisateurs entendent ainsi contribuer à une meilleure connaissance de l’histoire culturelle nationale, tout en encourageant une réflexion sur les moyens de faire de la musique et des autres disciplines artistiques des leviers de transmission, d’innovation et de création d’emplois.

items.title: The Atlantic ’s November Cover: Josh Tyrangiel Profiles Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk on Their Race to Control Outer Space—And Measures Who Is Ahead
items.description: In The Atlantic ’s November cover story, “ Choose Your Overlord ,” staff writer Josh Tyrangiel profiles Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk, who are in a race to control outer space. Tyrangiel writes that together, in fierce competition, “these two billionaires are in the early stages of a race to vertically integrate the galaxy—a process that involves rockets, moon landings, enormous satellite constellations, and space-based data centers running AI models fueled by computing power that no terrestrial supplier can match. Both say they hope to preserve human life from the specter of climate change and expand mankind’s understanding of the universe. Both would also like to dominate a market that, unlike every other market they’ve previously conquered, has no ceiling and few established rules.” For most of human history, Tyrangiel writes, “the power to decide where a civilization went next belonged to governments, monarchs, or despots. It’s a measure of how much has changed that a retail executive from Seattle and a South African–born engineer are well positioned to exercise that power. Nobody voted for either of them. And they may be the only ones who can check the other’s power.” But as Tyrangiel writes, one of them clearly has the upper hand. In 2025, Musk’s SpaceX launched 83 percent of the mass sent into orbit—about 10 times more than its nearest competitor, the Chinese government. His satellite company, Starlink, has 11,000-plus satellites, accounting for roughly two-thirds of all active spacecraft orbiting Earth. Tyrangiel points out that America “ needing Bezos’s extraordinary concentration of private power to mitigate Musk’s extraordinary concentration of private power is probably not what the Founders had in mind. ” When Tyrangiel asked Senator Mark Kelly, a former astronaut, whether he trusted either man completely, Kelly replied, “Kind of a loaded question.” Kelly, Tyrangiel reports, says he wants SpaceX to “continue to be a successful company because it is in our national-security interest that that’s the case. I also want to see Blue Origin be successful.” Tyrangiel writes: “The pragmatist’s position, shared by most of the national-security community, is that one company capable of getting you to space is better than none, and two is better than one. But even if Bezos is the less mercurial billionaire, Blue Origin is not yet a reliable substitute for SpaceX. So the government can’t use Blue Origin as leverage.” The government is not negotiating from a position of strength, but Tyrangiel writes, “Bezos and Musk have a shared vulnerability: Both say they would like to go to the moon—for their empires, for glory, and because their youthful love of space has never settled into something more rational. To put it in terms they and the president would all understand, the moon is leverage.” And in their race to the moon, Tyrangiel writes, “ most people I spoke with have reached the same conclusion: On this, Blue Origin is ahead. It has completed thermal-vacuum testing on Blue Moon, and, as of August, its structure, propulsion, and avionics were fully assembled; it’s already communicating with NASA’s satellites and deep-space network … The crux of the difference is that Blue Origin—the smaller, slower company in need of a win—seems to have built a product to fit the brief, while Musk has built a giant rocket designed for his satellite business and his personal goal of deep-space travel to Mars. Making Starship work for the moon is like adapting a cargo ship to win a yacht race.” Josh Tyrangiel’s “ Choose Your Overlord ” was published today at TheAtlantic.com. Please reach out with any questions or requests. Press contacts: Anna Bross and Paul Jackson | The Atlantic press@theatlantic.com

items.title: US, Canada, 8 other countries that allow Nigerians, other foreigners join their military
items.description: Foreign nationals seeking opportunities to serve in a foreign military can apply to join the armed forces of several countries, although eligibility depends on nationality, immigration status, military experience and the recruitment programme available. Countries such as France, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, Spain, the United States, Ukraine, Russia and New Zealand have provisions under which certain foreign nationals can serve in their armed forces. Israel also operates a special enlistment programme for eligible foreign volunteers. However, the rules differ considerably. While some countries accept foreign applicants without requiring permanent residency, others restrict recruitment to citizens of selected countries, permanent residents or experienced military personnel. For Nigerians considering military service abroad, understanding these differences is essential because being eligible to enlist does not automatically guarantee a visa, admission into the armed forces or permission to settle in the country. Here are nine countries, alongside Israel’s special volunteer programme, where foreign nationals may be eligible to serve in the military. 1. France France is among the best-known destinations for foreigners seeking to enlist in a foreign military through its French Foreign Legion. The Legion, a branch of the French Army, recruits men of different nationalities and allows eligible foreign nationals to apply without first becoming French citizens. According to the Legion’s official recruitment website, applicants must generally be older than 17 and younger than 40 when they report to a recruitment office. Candidates must also meet medical, physical and administrative requirements. Applicants from outside the Schengen area must present a passport, although the Legion does not arrange visas or exit authorisation on behalf of recruits. Unlike conventional recruitment into many national armed forces, the Foreign Legion has a specific recruitment system designed to accommodate foreign nationals. 2. United Kingdom The United Kingdom recruits eligible foreign nationals into its armed forces, including the British Army, subject to nationality and recruitment rules. Eligible applicants can include citizens of Commonwealth countries, a category that includes Nigeria, as well as Irish citizens and certain other groups. The British Army has historically recruited Commonwealth citizens and operates the Brigade of Gurkhas, which recruits eligible Nepalese applicants. However, Commonwealth citizenship alone does not guarantee admission. Recruitment availability, residency requirements, age limits, medical standards and the specific service or role can affect eligibility. The UK Ministry of Defence has also operated limited recruitment arrangements for Commonwealth applicants in specialist roles. Consequently, prospective applicants should check whether applications are currently open before making travel plans. 3. Australia Australia allows certain foreign nationals to apply to join the Australian Defence Force (ADF). Under eligibility arrangements introduced in 2024 and expanded from 2025, eligible permanent residents from the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada can apply. Eligible New Zealand citizens living in Australia can also apply. Applicants must satisfy additional requirements, including residency conditions, medical and physical standards, security checks and relevant citizenship rules. Australia also has an overseas lateral-entry pathway for eligible personnel with previous military experience whose skills can be transferred to the Australian Defence Force. This means Australia is not an unrestricted destination for anyone seeking to join a foreign military. Nationality, residency and previous service can determine whether an application is accepted. 4. Canada Canada permits eligible permanent residents, as well as Canadian citizens, to apply to join the Canadian Armed Forces. This creates a potential route for foreign nationals who have already obtained permanent residency in Canada. However, applicants must satisfy the armed forces’ recruitment conditions. The official recruitment website specifies that permanent resident applicants must provide evidence of three years of physical presence in Canada. Age, education, medical fitness, background checks and the requirements of the selected military occupation also apply. Therefore, Nigerians hoping to enlist in Canada generally need to establish the required immigration status and meet the applicable recruitment conditions before they can join. 5. Spain Spain allows certain foreign nationals to compete for places in its armed forces, particularly in enlisted soldier and sailor positions. However, eligibility is restricted to citizens of specified countries rather than foreigners generally. Spain’s 2026 recruitment documentation identifies eligible nationalities including Argentina, Bolivia, Colombia, Chile, Ecuador, Mexico, Peru, the Dominican Republic, Uruguay and Venezuela, alongside other listed countries. Equatorial Guinea and several other Spanish-speaking countries are also included. The number of places available to foreign applicants is limited, and candidates must satisfy age, education, criminal-record and other recruitment requirements. Nigeria is not among the nationalities listed in Spain’s 2026 recruitment rules for these foreign-applicant places. 6. United States The United States permits certain non-citizens to enlist in its military, but it does not generally offer ordinary enlistment to foreign nationals living overseas without the required immigration status. The US Army states that enlisted applicants must be US citizens or lawful permanent residents holding a valid Green Card, alongside other eligibility requirements. A Green Card provides permanent resident status, allowing eligible holders to live and work in the United States. Non-citizens who meet the requirements may subsequently qualify for an expedited naturalisation process through military service, subject to applicable law. However, military service is not a general visa programme, and a person cannot assume that applying to enlist will automatically provide permission to enter or reside in the United States. 7. Ukraine Ukraine permits foreign nationals and stateless persons to serve in its armed forces under military contracts. The country has recruited international volunteers during its war with Russia, including through its International Legion for the Defence of Ukraine. Ukraine’s official recruitment information states that foreign volunteers can serve as full members of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, with applicable service conditions, remuneration and benefits. Its foreign-national recruitment guidance says applicants must already be legally present in Ukraine to apply through the relevant Ground Forces recruitment route. Candidates are subject to background checks, medical examinations and other requirements. The official International Legion website also provides information for foreigners seeking to apply. However, prospective recruits must carefully consider the risks of military service in an active war zone, including the possibility of serious injury or death, as well as the legal implications of serving in a foreign armed force. 8. Russia Russia permits foreign nationals to enter military service under contract, subject to its laws and recruitment requirements. Russian legislation provides for foreign citizens and stateless persons to serve under military contracts. The legal framework has also been amended in recent years, including changes made in 2025. However, the existence of a legal route does not mean every foreign national is automatically eligible or that all recruitment offers are genuine. Anyone considering this option should independently verify the applicable law, contract terms, immigration requirements and consequences of military service. The risks associated with service during an international armed conflict also warrant particular attention. 9. New Zealand New Zealand operates an overseas recruitment pathway for certain applicants with military backgrounds. According to the New Zealand Defence Force’s overseas recruitment guidance, eligible candidates can include serving members of the armed forces of the United Kingdom, Australia, the United States and Canada who meet the applicable service-release conditions. The pathway also covers certain citizens of those countries who meet specified citizenship or residency criteria, provided they satisfy the relevant vacancy and rank requirements. This is principally a route for experienced military personnel rather than an open enlistment programme for all foreign civilians. Applicants must meet the Defence Force’s medical, security and professional requirements and obtain the necessary immigration status. 10. Israel: Special enlistment programme for foreign volunteers Israel provides a special route through which eligible foreign volunteers can serve in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) without first becoming Israeli citizens. The IDF identifies Mahal as an enlistment programme for foreign volunteers interested in serving in military combat and support roles. This is different from unrestricted recruitment into the Israeli military. Applicants must meet the programme’s eligibility requirements, and participation depends on the applicable rules and recruitment arrangements. The IDF also operates other programmes for foreign volunteers that involve supporting military activities without necessarily becoming full-time soldiers. Prospective applicants should distinguish between formal enlistment and non-combat volunteer programmes before applying. What Nigerians should know before applying Although these countries provide routes for certain foreign nationals to serve, the requirements vary substantially. Nationality: Some countries accept applicants from specified nationalities, while others have broader foreign-recruitment systems. Immigration status: Canada and the United States generally require applicants to hold permanent resident status if they are not citizens. Australia’s eligibility rules also impose nationality and residency conditions. Military experience: Some overseas recruitment pathways, particularly in New Zealand and Australia, are designed for people who have already served in the military. Age and fitness: Applicants must meet the relevant age limits, medical standards, physical requirements and background checks. Legal consequences: Serving in a foreign military may have implications under the applicant’s home-country laws. Nigerians should seek reliable legal advice before signing a contract with a foreign armed force. Recruitment scams: Applicants should use official military recruitment websites and verify any offer before paying fees or sharing sensitive documents. items.title: NUC introduces post-accreditation monitoring, admission checks to varsities
items.description: By Joseph Erunke, Abuja The National Universities Commission (NUC) is stepping up regulatory oversight of Nigerian universities, introducing fresh quality assurance measures targeting admission processes, academic standards, accreditation and institutional governance amid growing concerns over the quality and global competitiveness of university education. The Executive Secretary of the commission, Prof. Abdullahi Yusufu Ribadu, disclosed this on Tuesday in Abuja at the opening of the 2026 NUC retreat with vice-chancellors of all Nigerian universities. Among the measures being pursued by the commission are post-accreditation monitoring visits to universities, post-matriculation monitoring and carrying-capacity visits to improve admission processes, and the development of accreditation software to enhance transparency, data management and regulatory compliance. Ribadu also announced plans to develop a national artificial intelligence roadmap and policy framework for the Nigerian University System, alongside efforts to strengthen research commercialisation and translate university research into practical solutions for national development. The two-day retreat, which brought together vice-chancellors of federal, state and private universities, is themed “Enhancing Regulatory Compliance, Governance, Leadership, and Partnership in the Nigerian University System”. The renewed push for tighter oversight comes as Nigerian universities grapple with funding constraints, technological disruption, questions of academic quality and the need to produce graduates equipped with the skills required by a rapidly changing economy. Speaking at the event, the Minister of State for Education, Prof. Suwaiba Said Ahmad, said improving the university system required stronger compliance with regulatory directives, transparent institutional administration and closer collaboration between the NUC and university managements. Ahmad, who declared the retreat open, said universities could no longer rely on isolated institutional efforts or regulatory directives alone to overcome the challenges confronting higher education. She said sustained engagement between the regulator and university leadership was necessary to ensure coherent policy implementation and make institutions more responsive to national priorities and global developments. According to her, the growing influence of artificial intelligence, digital learning, data analytics, virtual laboratories, research and innovation requires universities to rethink their operations while safeguarding academic integrity, ethics and data protection. The minister stressed that vice-chancellors must demonstrate accountability in financial management, procurement, recruitment, promotion, admissions and examinations. She urged university heads to establish clear institutional visions, set measurable performance targets and create environments conducive to academic excellence. Ahmad said the retreat should go beyond discussions to produce practical commitments capable of delivering measurable improvements across the university system. She expressed support for the proposed communiqué and post-retreat monitoring mechanism, describing them as important instruments for ensuring that resolutions reached at the meeting translate into concrete institutional action. Ahmad similarly warned that the adoption of AI must be accompanied by safeguards for academic integrity, responsible use, ethics and data protection. In his address, Ribadu said the commission had strengthened its operational guidelines since he assumed office on December 23, 2024, as part of efforts to improve the quality and relevance of university education. He disclosed that the NUC had introduced post-matriculation monitoring and carrying-capacity visits to universities to improve admission processes and ensure institutions operated within appropriate capacity limits. The commission, he added, was preparing to institute post-accreditation monitoring visits to strengthen the implementation of quality assurance standards after academic programmes had secured accreditation. Ribadu also announced the development of new guidelines for the award and use of honorary doctorate degrees, including sanctions for universities that violate the rules. He said the NUC Policy Development Strategy Committee had completed a comprehensive review and produced Blueprint 2.0 for the Rapid Revitalisation of Nigerian University Education. The commission is also developing a 21st-century strategic plan and transitioning from the Annual Performance Evaluation system to a Performance Monitoring System pioneered by the Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation. Ribadu urged universities to strengthen institutional strategic planning, warning that sustainable improvements in academic standards required deliberate planning, effective leadership and continuous monitoring. The NUC boss said artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies were reshaping how knowledge was created, delivered and accessed, making digital transformation imperative for Nigerian universities. He disclosed that the commission had developed and deployed the e-NUC platform to automate its entire workflow, while accreditation software was being developed to improve the efficiency and transparency of quality assurance processes. He, however, cautioned that digital transformation must go beyond the acquisition of hardware and software to include institutional preparedness, staff capacity development, cybersecurity and appropriate policies. Ribadu also said the commission was developing a national AI roadmap and policy framework for universities, stressing the need to ensure that technological adoption was responsible, relevant and aligned with national development priorities. Beyond regulation and technology, Ribadu called for stronger collaboration between universities, government, industry and other stakeholders to ensure that research outcomes translated into products, services and solutions addressing Nigeria’s development challenges. He identified agriculture, healthcare, education, technology, manufacturing, the environment and the creative industry as areas where university research should have tangible economic and social impact. According to him, the commission had launched the ACE Alliance platform to strengthen collaboration among Nigeria’s 20 African Centres of Excellence and unveiled a four-volume compendium documenting research outputs from the centres. He also disclosed that the Tertiary Education Research and Application Services platform of the Tertiary Education Trust Fund had been integrated with the Nigerian Research and Education Network at the directive of the Minister of Education to encourage research collaboration. Ribadu said the commission was establishing a Research Commercialisation Division to strengthen the protection of intellectual property and the conversion of viable research findings into marketable products. He added that the NUC was working towards an international study tour for selected vice-chancellors to universities in Europe and Asia to examine global best practices in research commercialisation. Acknowledging the financial challenges confronting the university system, Ribadu said inadequate resources remained a major obstacle to institutional development. He urged universities to explore innovative resource mobilisation strategies, including partnerships with the private sector, alumni associations and development partners, while ensuring that such arrangements complied with regulatory requirements and institutional objectives. He disclosed that the NUC had established partnerships with development agencies, including the World Bank, the Agence Française de Développement and the African Development Bank, to attract additional support for university development. The commission, he said, would continue to work with relevant stakeholders to reposition Nigerian universities for excellence and global competitiveness. Retreat to produce an implementation roadmap. Ribadu said the retreat was convened to provide a platform for frank discussions on the challenges facing higher education, the effectiveness of existing policies and the practical steps required to improve institutional performance. He urged vice-chancellors to demonstrate integrity, accountability, courage and consensus-building in managing their institutions, adding that university leadership must be guided by institutional priorities and established due processes. Earlier, the Chairman of the Local Organising Committee and Director of Research, Innovation and Information Technology Transfer at the NUC, Lawal Mohammed Faruk, said the retreat was designed to strengthen relations between the commission and universities through strategic engagement. Faruk identified its objectives as strengthening regulatory compliance and quality assurance, advancing good governance and transformational leadership, and building strategic partnerships for the development of university education. The meeting is expected to culminate in a communiqué outlining agreed policy actions and institutional commitments, with a post-retreat monitoring and feedback mechanism proposed to track implementation. items.title: Nouvelles mesures fortes pour le sport burkinabè : Thérapie de choc pour un grand corps malade !
items.description: (Ouagadougou, 13 octobre 2026). Le Président du Faso, Chef de l’État, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ a rencontré, le lundi 12 octobre dans la matinée, les Gouverneurs de région et les responsables sportifs afin de leur donner des orientations sur l’organisation de la Ligue de la Souveraineté. La Ligue de la Souveraineté est née de la volonté du Camarade Président du Faso, Chef de l’État, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ de refonder le milieu du sport burkinabè. L'objectif est d'assurer une meilleure répartition géographique de l'offre sportive sur l'ensemble du territoire national. Ce championnat qui voit ainsi le jour repose en partie sur les régions, d’où la tenue de cette rencontre avec les Gouverneurs de région, en présence de la Ministre des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi, Camarade Annick Lydie Djouma PIKBOUGOUM/ZINGUÉ OUATTARA, de la Ministre déléguée chargée du Budget, Camarade Fatoumata BAKO/TRAORÉ, du président de la délégation spéciale de la Chambre de commerce et d’industrie, Camarade Roland Achille SOW, d’un représentant du Patronat burkinabè, Camarade Alassane SIENOU et des anciens internationaux Charles KABORÉ, ambassadeur pour le sport, Sibiri Alain TRAORÉ et Adama GUIRA. « Il faut impliquer les régions parce que nous avons décidé de donner de l’identité à notre sport. Et la compétition se crée aussi ainsi. S’il n’y a pas d’identité, ce à quoi il faut s’attacher pour supporter un athlète, une équipe, ce sera difficile », a soutenu le Président du Faso, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ. « Votre responsabilité première est engagée. Ce sera à vous de coordonner pour pouvoir recruter les entraineurs, d’effectuer les championnats au niveau régional pour pouvoir faire la sélection des jeunes joueurs qui feront partie de l’équipe », a indiqué le Président du Faso. Près de 1000 emplois créés pour un salaire minimum de 200 000 fcfa/mois Il a également annoncé la mise en place d’un dispositif de médiatisation du championnat, tout en mettant en garde contre « les faux deals ». Chaque athlète sélectionné aura une retribution minimale de 200 000 fcfa avec des avantages connexes. Près de 1000 emplois seront ainsi créés. Contribution volontaire mais obligatoire du secteur privé Outre les Gouverneurs, le Président du Faso a invité les opérateurs économiques à apporter un soutien au fonctionnement. « Ce sera une contribution volontaire mais obligatoire au niveau de chaque région pour soutenir le sport » a déclaré le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ. À travers la Ligue de la Souveraineté, le Chef de l’État entend offrir un cadre d’expression aux jeunes dans plusieurs disciplines sportives et du même coup lutter contre certains fléaux comme la consommation de la drogue et de l’alcool. « On ne peut pas construire une Nation avec une jeunesse qui est malade, avec une jeunesse qui n’est pas consciente. La Révolution veut refonder notre Patrie en se basant sur nos ressources. Et les ressources que nous avons sous la main c’est la jeunesse », a dit le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ. Pour valoriser cette richesse que sont les jeunes, le Président du Faso mise également sur le sport pour « les modeler, les garder sains de corps, pour avoir un esprit sain ». items.title: Govt says people of KP ‘welcomed’ governor's rule as it gave them ‘hope’
items.description: Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Tuesday claimed that the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had “welcomed” the federal government’s move to impose governor’s rule and emergency in the province, saying the measures had given them “hope”. The federal government on Sunday imposed an emergency in 12 districts of KP, and placed the province under governor’s rule, taking note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. On Tuesday, Attaullah addressed a joint press conference alongside Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar in Islamabad. Attaullah noted, “Had the people of KP supported the pro-terrorist stance of the PTI government, you would have seen millions on the street.” He went on to claim that “barely a dozen” people had gathered in protest. Defending the move, the information minister said: “The people of KP have welcomed the step because they believe there is now hope for them. They believe they will now be provided with safety and security, their lives and livelihoods will be protected, and this political-crime nexus will be eliminated.” At the outset of the press briefing, the law minister noted that the province in the recent past had witnessed a hike in terrorist incidents, noting a “195 per cent” rise, with 8,600 terrorist attacks recorded in 2024-2026 compared to 2,900 in 2020-2024. Azam emphasised that it was essential that counterterrorism efforts taken by federal and provincial agencies be “harmonised”, adding that such an approach was standard practice globally. “All these arrangements are made to run the country in a way that people feel safe,” he remarked. At this, the law minister noted the “non-serious” attitude of the previous PTI-led KP government, which he said, “has now ceased to exist”. He recalled that the PTI, allegedly using government resources, “launched an onslaught on the capital”. However, at the time, the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency did not come under discussion. Describing the situation on the ground in the province, the law minister said: “The KP police were under attack, armed forces deployed in the province were under attack […] innocent people lost their lives.” “You cannot shut your eyes after receiving such reports and seeing this rise in terrorist activity,” Azam added. Recalling the events leading up to the federal government’s decision, Azam said the government had held “constant engagement” with the provincial authorities. “Unfortunately, their response was somewhat different. Maybe their politics were more important to them than having the national interest at heart,” he said. He maintained that the federal government had exhausted “all possible avenues” to resolve the differences. Azam said the provincial government should have intervened amid “internal disturbances or the likelihood or apprehension of such disturbances”. Referring to Article 232, under which the emergency was imposed, Azam said it “deals with internal disturbances where the law and order situation is such, and the onslaught is of a nature that the provincial government cannot fight against it”. Referring to the PTI, he said, “Your priorities were not to curb terrorism or to fight against it”. “In such grave conditions, your priority should be to protect the people, not to pursue political gains.” Azam said it was against this backdrop that the prime minister brought the matter before the federal cabinet, and a decision was subsequently made. On being asked why similar measures could not be enacted in Balochistan, despite the prevailing security situation in the province, Azam said: “Look at the conduct of the Balochistan government; the chief minister is on his toes [..] he is trying hard.” He noted that whenever there is a terrorist incident in Balochistan, the CM visits the area himself and personally oversees relief efforts. ‘Total breakdown of governance’ Attaullah, during the presser, reiterated that the federal government did not have a political agenda against the PTI-led provincial government; instead, it was pursuing “a unified policy on counterterrorism”. “You cannot have a government in the country that sympathises with terrorists, supports terrorism or has a policy that enables terrorists to carry out their operational actions,” he said. He questioned how one country could have two separate counterterrorism policies. “As the [law] minister explained, the framers of the constitution included these clauses (232 and 234) for a time like this,” citing a “complete breakdown” of law and order in KP. The minister went on to question why resources allocated to the provincial government via the National Finance Commission Award were not utilised to strengthen security-related infrastructure and equip KP police. The information minister reiterated that the PTI-led government was facilitating the terrorists, describing it as a “political-terrorist nexus”. He further said there was a “total breakdown of governance” in KP, noting a lack of reforms in education, health, and public services. Vawda touts ‘reboot’ Separately, Independent Senator Faisal Vawda reappeared on television following the recent political developments and touted the governor’s rule as the beginning of a “reboot” of the country’s governance. Addressing a press conference at the National Press Club in Islamabad, the former PTI member described the new set-up in KP as a “good cabinet”, but also stressed that it must show its performance before its 180-day tenure. “It will be performance-based; if they are not able to perform, better ones will come,” Vawda said. “Failure is no option,” he emphasised, saying the governor-run administration will face even stricter scrutiny. Vawda remarked, “Through this province, God willing, in the story of Pakistan … we are looking into the option of reboot, not that boot but the mobile one.” Responding to a query about his “reboot” metaphor, the senator said such a format usually entails “deletion, subtraction and addition” of individuals. Referring to the eight PTI leaders in preventative detention, he said, “Eight men were with me in the last 48 hours, including their cabinet members.” However, he claimed, “All of them are involved in the arrests; all of them staged a drama.” Addressing PTI leaders, he said, “Some of them will be left, some of them will be picked up, some will be washed away. The party is already scattered; it’s all over. The show is over.” Later in his media talk, Vawda declared: “PTI, as of now, does not exist anymore; neither will.” Vawda also rejected allegations against Maulana Fazlur Rehman — who made efforts to reduce tensions between the Centre and PTI — that he “trapped” Sohail Afridi by inviting him to talks at CM House. Asked about his thoughts on ex-premier Imran Khan’s future, the former PTI leader said the former taught him politics. “It is the same politics that I am doing today,” he added. Emergency over terrorism concerns On Sunday, the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and governor’s rule under Article 234. The decision came during a meeting of the federal cabinet, which deliberated on the security situation in PTI-led KP and noted the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. Subsequently, the prime minister sent a summary to the president, who approved the move. Soon after, the Centre also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. Meanwhile, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre sought to explain that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. On Monday, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar defended the governor’s rule, saying it was not politically motivated but instead taken to curb terrorism. The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.

items.title: BAD/Rapport pays 2026: la bonne santé des indicateurs macroéconomiques témoigne de la résilience économique du Burkina
items.description: Ceci est un Rapport pays 2026 élaboré par la BAD qui soutient que « malgré les difficultés, la bonne santé des indicateurs macroéconomiques témoigne de la résilience économique du Burkina Faso, affirmant que « le principal défi reste de faire ressentir les retombées de cette performance dans le secteur social ». « Classé parmi les pays à faible revenu, le Burkina Faso est confronté à une vulnérabilité structurelle. L’enclavement, la question sécuritaire, la crise humanitaire, l’impact du changement climatique et les tensions géopolitiques régionales et internationales, constituent les principales contraintes qui entravent le développement socio-économique du pays. Malgré les difficultés, la bonne santé des indicateurs macroéconomiques témoigne de la résilience économique du Burkina Faso. Le principal défi reste de faire ressentir les retombées de cette performance dans le secteur social. L’économie demeure sur une trajectoire positive, ce qui pourrait augurer d’une amélioration à terme des conditions de vie des populations. Dans le cadre de la mise en oeuvre du Plan national de développement RELANCE 2026-2030, le pays devrait mobiliser des financements de développement de grande ampleur, pour pouvoir maintenir ce dynamisme des activités économiques et avoir un impact social fort. Avec la tendance globale à la baisse de l’Aide publique au développement (APD) et le durcissement des conditions d’accès aux financements internationaux, une stratégie volontariste et cohérente de mobilisation des financements s’impose pour tirer profit des opportunités de mobilisation des financements internes et attirer aussi des investissements de l’extérieur. Le Rapport pays 2026 de la Banque africaine de développement intitulé « Mobiliser des ressources à grande échelle pour le financement du Burkina Faso dans un monde fragmenté », tente d’apporter des pistes de réflexion dans le cadre de cette mobilisation massive des financements au développement pour le pays. Il se donne pour ambition de reproduire, au niveau du pays, les analyses effectuées aux niveaux continental et régional dans le rapport principal des Perspectives économiques en Afrique (PEA) de 2026 de la Banque africaine de développement sur le même thème. Le rapport s’articule comme suit: Le chapitre 1 met en lumière la performance macroéconomique récente et les projections économiques du Burkina Faso. Le chapitre 2 explore les mécanismes de mobilisation à grande échelle des financements du développement au Burkina Faso, dans un contexte mondial fragmenté. Quant au chapitre 3, il examine les stratégies visant à consolider et à renforcer le système financier et les acteurs au Burkina Faso face aux mutations mondiales. Chaque chapitre formule des recommandations stratégiques à l’attention du pays et des banques multilatérales de développement. » Cliquez ici pour lire l'intégralité du RAPPORT PAYS 2026 BURKINA FASO de la BAD L’article BAD/Rapport pays 2026: la bonne santé des indicateurs macroéconomiques témoigne de la résilience économique du Burkina est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Boubacar Yacine Diallo: l’État au cœur, l’éthique en boussole, la fidélité en crédo
items.description: Nous sommes le 13 octobre 2026 à Conakry. Les projecteurs brûlent. La tempête gronde. Dans l'arène du pouvoir et de la vérité, peu d'hommes résistent au choc. Un vrai leader n'accuse jamais les circonstances ou les autres. Il assume pleinement ses responsabilités et cherche sans relâche des solutions. Le leadership ne consiste pas seulement à imposer une voix. Il s'agit de savoir écouter pour comprendre et guider. C'est précisément cette philosophie qui façonne le parcours exemplaire d'un homme devenu indissociable de l'histoire contemporaine des médias africains. Mais qui est cet homme qui ne tergiverse pas, ne tremble pas, ne décide pas de manière exagérée et n'écrase jamais pour plaire, mais pour aider et élever ? Lui, c'est Boubacar Yacine Diallo à l'état civil. Président de la Haute Autorité de la Communication de Guinée élu par acclamation à la présidence de la Plateforme des Régulateurs de l'Audiovisuel des pays membres de l'UEMOA et de la Guinée lors de la 12ᵉ Assemblée générale tenue à Conakry en août et septembre 2026, Boubacar Yacine Diallo personnifie la figure achevée du « sage des sages ». Formé à la bonne école, expérimenté et respecté, il demeure une personnalité indispensable tant au paysage médiatique guinéen qu’à celui de toute la sous-région. Modèle d'investigation et pionnier républicain Grand reporter d'exception et écrivain chevronné, Boubacar Yacine Diallo est entré dans l’histoire journalistique par un acte de courage mémorable : l'enquête éclairée qui a permis de faire déguerpir les déchets industriels toxiques largués aux îles de Loos sous le régime du président Lansana Conté. Réaliser un tel exploit en tant que journaliste employé de la fonction publique à la Radio Télévision Guinéenne relevait d'une audace républicaine sans pareille. C’est ce même esprit de visionnaire qui le poussera plus tard à convaincre les autorités de faire évoluer la Radio Télévision Guinéenne vers le statut d'Office, modernisant ainsi le service public de l'information. Ce parcours remarquable prend ses racines dans la ville carrefour de Mamou, où il effectue un brillant cursus scolaire et coranique. Admis à l'Institut polytechnique Julius Nyerere de Kankan en philosophie-histoire, puis transféré à l'université Gamal Abdel Nasser de Conakry, le jeune étudiant se distingue immédiatement. Alors qu'il s'apprête à soutenir son mémoire sur « Le matérialisme dans les œuvres du Parti Démocratique de Guinée – Rassemblement Démocratique Africain de Sékou Touré », il décroche une bourse d'études internationales en journalisme en Roumanie, cofinancée par l'Organisation des Nations unies pour l'éducation, la science et la culture. Rentré diplômé en 1982, affecté au journal parlé de « La Voix de la Révolution », le jeune Boubacar Yacine Diallo suscite d'abord la jalousie de sa hiérarchie. Pourtant, loin des querelles d'égos, il trace son sillon. Il privilégie le terrain, initie des reportages novateurs, couvre le chef de l'État et s'impose en rédigeant des commentaires percutants. Avec l'avènement du régime militaire en 1984, il introduit l'investigation comme genre majeur, révélant notamment le scandale des déchets toxiques et des détournements à la direction générale des Douanes. Repéré par le président Lansana Conté pour son intégrité, il accède à la rédaction en chef du journal parlé en 1991. Promu membre fondateur du Conseil National de la Communication en 1992 pour présider la commission d'éthique, puis Directeur Général de l'Office de la Radio Télévision Guinéenne en 1997, il fait preuve d'une dignité rare en démissionnant en 2000 par clause de conscience. Cette indépendance d'esprit le conduit à lancer le journal L'Enquêteur en 2002, avant d'être rappelé au sommet de l'État pour présider le CNC (Conseil National de la Communication) en 2005, puis de servir comme conseiller en communication du président Sékouba Konaté en 2010. Consacré président de l'URTELGUI (Union des Radiodiffusions et Télévisions Libres de Guinée) en 2009, ancien président du conseil d'administration de la Maison de la Presse et de président l’AGEPI (Association Guinéenne des Éditeurs de la Presse Indépendante), puis membre de l’INIDH (Institution Nationale Indépendante des Droits Humains) en 2014, il n'a cessé de défendre la liberté de la presse tout en rappelant la responsabilité des acteurs du secteur. Pour Boubacar Yacine Diallo, le leadership ne consiste pas seulement à imposer une voix, mais à savoir écouter pour comprendre et guider. Cet homme d'expérience est aussi un homme entier et d'une fidélité inébranlable, qui n'oublie jamais ses bienfaiteurs. Dans les moments difficiles, il sait comment dire la vérité avec courage et pédagogie pour aider à la fois son nouveau bienfaiteur tout en tirant d'affaires son ancien bienfaiteur. À cet égard, le cas de notre confrère et ancien ministre Tibou Kamara est révélateur : le président Boubacar Yacine Diallo a publiquement rappelé qu'il lui restait fidèle et redevable, une sortie médiatique empreinte d'élégance qui a profondément marqué l'opinion. De même, lorsque certaines décisions courageuses prises en toute collégialité par la Haute Autorité de la Communication font l'objet de commentaires au sein de la presse nationale et internationale, comme la mise en demeure suivie de la sanction contre France 24 ou les recadrages déontologiques appliqués à certains journalistes, l'analyse objective démontre toujours la touche et le sens élevé de la responsabilité d'un homme qui a eu le privilège d'exercer le métier aussi bien dans le secteur public que dans le privé. Il sait allier rigueur de la loi et soutien confraternel, sans jamais abdiquer devant les dérives. Auteur prolifique de plusieurs ouvrages majeurs consacrés à l’histoire politique nationale, dont Yacine Diallo, Premier Député guinéen et Il va pleuvoir sur Conakry, il demeure un repère moral indispensable. C’est tout à son honneur, et c’est tout en l’honneur de la Guinée républicaine et continue, du président fondateur Ahmed Sékou Touré jusqu’au président Mamadi Doumbouya. Ce qu'il fallait démontrer. Traverser les époques sans jamais renier ses principes fondamentaux demeure le privilège exclusif des véritables bâtisseurs de la République. « Être en avant et diriger expose aux critiques, aux pressions et aux difficultés les plus rudes. » Cette réalité exigente a constamment jalonné le parcours d'exception de Boubacar Yacine Diallo, lui dont chaque arbitrage reste guidé par une sagesse ancestrale selon laquelle « celui qui écoute apprend plus que celui qui parle. » Alliant le devoir d'impartialité, la hauteur de vue, l'intégrité déontologique et la loyauté institutionnelle, cet éminent homme d'État inscrit durablement sa mémoire au panthéon des grandes figures républicaines. Ainsi, Boubacar Yacine Diallo reste et demeure l'homme qui a l’État au cœur, l’éthique en boussole, la fidélité en crédo. Ibrahima Diallo, journaliste et écrivain.

items.title: The Rise of the IRL Influencer
items.description: At Café Soul, a semi-regular party in New York City, $30 buys you a chance to belt R&B hits, sip margaritas from commemorative glasses, try out Awkward Games’ icebreaker cards, and—as the ticket page promises—form “genuine connections.” When I arrived 45 minutes after the rooftop party started on a recent Saturday afternoon, the few 20- and 30-something guests were mostly sitting on mid-century modern couches, looking at their phones. But Tionne Barmer, who dreamed up the event, promised me that, in two hours, the rooftop would be packed: People would be enjoying the Patrón-sponsored bar, trying the brown-sugar cold brew (underwritten by On the Way Coffee), using Awkward Games cards to skip small talk, and maybe even flirting. (The event was also sponsored by Tinder.) They’d have a chance to make genuine connections, which is what Barmer was really selling. “People will pay for the entertainment,” he said, “and, on the side, they get community.” Barmer has always had a talent for bringing people together, and now he’s making a living out of it. Some people call this job “event curator”; others have started using the term community builder . People like Barmer are, in essence, professional scene-makers. They were student-body presidents, sorority leaders, slumber-party queens, that one guy in the friend group who threw the best parties—and now they organize knitting circles , silent reading parties , adult summer camps , run clubs , and life-story sharing sessions to help young adults find one another. They sell their guests the opportunity for friendship, and they sell brands access to the groups they’ve gathered, not on Instagram or TikTok, but in real life. If Barmer and others like him can make this a full-time profession (he quit his finance job only when his side gig as a community builder could match that income), it’s in part because Americans are in desperate need of shindigs. As The Atlantic has reported , in the past three decades, pretty much every measure of socializing—hosting dinner parties, going on picnics, volunteering—has dropped by double digits; in 2023, only 4.1 percent of us managed to make it to a social event or host one on an average weekend or holiday. “Everyone wants to attend parties, but no one wants to throw them,” Ellen Cushing wrote in this magazine last year. Planning a party is, after all, a lot of work. Umama Kibria, a co-founder of Play Social Club, grew up helping her father host picnics for their Desi community. He’d cater meals and create elaborate The Price Is Right –esque games. Although he sold tickets to cover the cost of the food, he’d spend his own money on the decor, activities, and prizes. Kibria saw how the events drained his energy and finances. When she graduated from college, she started hosting large gatherings of her own, including grown-up field days and her own Desi picnics. Unlike her dad, she charged enough to make a profit. What really shocked her father, Kibria told me, was how she was able to find brand partners who’d contribute $10,000 sponsorships so that she could periodically host free events. Between ticket sales, affiliated codes, equity deals, and consulting gigs, she made her dad’s hobby her full-time job. If she provides her peers with the social life they crave, she realized, “people will pay.” They really will, Joan Li, an associate principal of wellness-industry insights at the market-research firm Mintel, told me. Many Americans now see social connection as a purchasable good. Just as DoorDash offers food delivery for people who don’t have time or don’t want to cook, solo entrepreneurs and businesses offer social calendars. This so-called IRL economy is in some ways a reaction against the internet and the ills of the influencer economy: People want to get off their phones and go somewhere to make an actual friend. But the job of “community builder” is also an outgrowth of influencer culture, Brooke Erin Duffy, a communications professor at Cornell who studies influencers, told me. Because social media is now saturated with creators monetizing their followers, anyone who can get people together offline and in-person could command a premium. That’s part of the pitch that Pie (short for “People I Enjoy”), a new platform for hosts to advertise and monetize events, is making. “Think about the value of how much influencers get paid to make a video to, hopefully, get someone for three-to-five seconds in a feed, versus sticking someone IRL in front of a logo or a product for an hour. The value is so much higher there,” Nadya Okamoto, an influencer and a co-founder of Pie, told me. The thought of Michaels sponsoring knitting circles so that the company can stick its logo in front of people for longer might give some of us pause—it certainly bummed me out—but Pie, along with agencies such as Onbrand and Offline, which match brands with events to sponsor, are pushing to build a world in which socializing is also a marketing opportunity. Right now, Pie offers participants in its Pie Creator Club, including Barmer, an average of $445 and up to $3,500 a month to organize gatherings. The company also co-hosted a dinner this summer at which community builders swapped best practices for “communitymaxxing.” It’s currently using venture capital to pay its creators, but long-term, Pie is wagering that businesses will pay community builders like they do online influencers, for access to their guests. And some brands are already betting on this new economy: Tinder launched an “Events” section of its app this past spring, and by the end of the year, plans to feature events in 75 cities, mainly through partnerships with party organizers like Barmer. As I wandered around Café Soul, which was part of a series that Barmer had designed to get people off their phones, signs reminded guests to LIVE IN THE MOMENT. And as the party picked up, they were doing just that: Hundreds of people formed a dance circle, then opened it up for a man in head-to-toe stone-washed denim, who dropped it low, backed it up, and gave his new friends what may be one of the most electric performances of T-Pain’s “I’m Sprung” ever given at 3 p.m. on a Saturday. But people did also have their phones out to film themselves dancing and lip-syncing; one guy in plaid culottes and tiny green sunglasses was filming on a tripod. These events still need to generate online content to be financially viable, Andrew Roth, a co-founder of Offline, told me. Most people find out about these communities through social media, and companies expect that any event they sponsor will generate posts featuring their products. Still, he said, influencers get paid millions of dollars to keep us on our phones—why not reward the hosts getting us (mostly) off them? Roth described a future in which “you already have your monthly book club, and it just so happens this one you’re going to get paid for.” This proposition is akin to an older phenomenon—the Tupperware parties of the 1950s, Duffy said, when women hosted friends in their living room and exhibited the latest and greatest in food storage. Plenty of people have also paid to socialize at their country club or local Rotary chapter; others have found ways to turn their hobbies into a business, without a venture-backed app to help them do it. At its worst, a world in which a book club is sponsored by Barefoot Wine could make people feel like their every waking moment is a marketing opportunity, even more than they already do. When I played a round of icebreaker cards with two women—who had first met, they told me, at a makeup class at Nordstrom, hosted by another so-called IRL community called Girls That Gather—I had fun, but I felt a bit like I was inhabiting a simulacrum of “community.” Yet all the hosts I spoke with seemed like they were earnestly trying to make sure that their events did not feel that way. Many of them asked me which communities I was a part of. I’d tell them about Sundays at church and Wednesday Bible study in my living room. A couple of them told me that they were essentially trying to build a secular community from the same template: Churches give people a physical place to repeatedly congregate in a large group setting, and also offer ways for smaller groups to gather throughout the week. Safi Aziz, another full-time community builder, told me he sees events as helping fill the gap left by the decline of public institutions. “If we’re no longer gathering as much over religion” or other organizational ties, he said, “all we really have left to gather over is common interest.” (In his case, that common interest is game nights, which he runs through his company, Joust.) But unlike these IRL communities, church doesn’t promise a great time. Authentic communities can’t be optimized, because they’re fueled by friction: showing up when it is inconvenient; being kind to one another even when Barbara is being a pain in the neck. They build trust because they ask something of you, besides just money, as the price of admission. So far, professional community builders mostly seem to be offering people an easy way to party—and thank God for that. Even if someone goes to an event and doesn’t connect with anyone, they’ve still gathered with a group of people that weekend. That is the first step of being part of a community, and something America certainly needs.

items.title: Good Villains Are Hard to Come By. This One’s Great.
items.description: Villains, in 21st-century literature, are hard to come by. Very few novelists write real Bad Guys or build their books around clear struggles between good and evil—and with reason. Such storylines, when executed poorly, can easily become didactic; a villain can turn into a cartoon. Yet some of the most satisfying stories out there, the ones that people have adapted and retold for centuries, are tales of good versus evil: Paradise Lost , Le Morte d’Arthur , a decent chunk of the Brothers Grimm. As recently as the mid-20th century, literary novelists were still writing evil characters: “Big Bads,” we might call them. Yet the gap between the sinister Cathy in John Steinbeck’s East of Eden and the somewhat redeemed version—the girl boss of the brothel, as The New Yorker ’s Alexandra Schwartz recently put it —in Zoe Kazan’s new Netflix adaptation indicates that writers are leery of villains now. Reading the canon suggests that this might foreclose on a rich vein of drama and meaning. So does reading the distinctly contemporary work of the Appalachian writer Madeline ffitch. ffitch is a longtime environmental activist, and her 2019 debut novel, Stay and Fight , follows three women raising a child off the grid in eastern Ohio while battling a natural-gas company that becomes their nemesis. Still, though the company has a slimy functionary, it’s essentially an impersonal version of evil. But in her newly released follow-up, Avalon, Rise , ffitch gives her villain a face and a voice. The novel is again set in Appalachian Ohio, in a small town where an internet-famous neo-Nazi has just moved. Its characters have to struggle against not only the extremist herself, but also her quickly spreading influence, while still dealing with their preexisting troubles, which include isolation, addiction, and one mother’s seeming compulsion to hit her child. These are serious matters—and yet some of the clearest influences in Avalon, Rise are children’s books. In fact, Pete Seeger’s Abiyoyo , the tale of a boy and his father who save their village from a giant, seems to be the book’s guiding star. Avalon, Rise is a sophisticated novel, intellectually complex and slyly funny at every turn. Like Abiyoyo , it is also a very direct story about facing evil with courage. Avalon, Rise makes the case on nearly every page that opposing the Big Bad is necessary. But that basic principle, the book suggests, does not make standing up to those who would destroy a community easy. Indeed, the ever-shifting balance between clarity and complication is central to the novel. ffitch is able to maintain this balance largely because she seems to have little interest in demonstrating purity—either her own or that of her characters. Avalon, Rise doesn’t care if its characters do the precisely correct thing. As a result, it achieves the rare feat of having a distinct sense of right and wrong, without ever becoming preachy or heavy-handed. It becomes an exploration of how confusing and hard it is to be good. Abiyoyo is set in a village united, as one of Avalon, Rise ’s characters puts it, by annoyance and fear. The annoyance is at the dad and son, who are such inconsiderate neighbors that the town exiles them; the fear is of Abiyoyo, a perhaps-mythical man-eating giant. But when Abiyoyo actually shows up one morning, the ostracized father-son duo comes up with a clever strategy to defeat him, saving the town and redeeming themselves in the process. All of these plot points—and really, these characters—appear in ffitch’s novel. In Avalon, Rise , the village is Avalon, Ohio, which seems to be loosely based on the real town of Athens. Its menacing giant is white nationalism, embodied by a true believer named Stasia—the “Volk Mother” or “OdinistMama” online—who moves to Avalon and begins recruiting in its community. But rather than having one parent and a child to defeat the villain, ffitch fills Avalon, Rise with a sprawling, endearing, enraging group of characters who are, if not outcasts, distinctly at the town’s margins. There’s Avalon’s social worker, who holds herself a bit apart from the community she serves; there’s the wishy-washy librarian who, by trying to agree with everyone she talks with, ends up going back constantly on her word; there are the anti-fascist organizers with bad attitudes and too many piercings. Over the course of the novel, which has the conviction of a manifesto but the relaxed, raucous narrative quality of a good shaggy-dog story, ffitch gets all of these characters to come together to deal not only with Stasia but also with the residents of Avalon who are willing, and in some cases eager, to enable her. [ Read: A diagnosis for social conflict that gets lost along the way ] Stasia’s leading enabler, Woody, is, perhaps counterintuitively, also Avalon, Rise ’s moral center. What I mean is that he’s the character who struggles the hardest. He is a printmaker and an addict (any reader who was disappointed, as I was, by Barbara Kingsolver’s Demon Copperhead will get a more nuanced and less dramatic portrait of drug addiction in Appalachia here). His prized possession is a milk crate of children’s books—including, pointedly, Abiyoyo— that he refers to regularly as sources of artistic inspiration, comfort during withdrawal, entertainment for his 4- and 7-year-old nephews, and guidance for when he doesn’t know what to do. Woody gets sucked into Stasia’s orbit after she commissions him to print flyers for her “European Heritage Rug Braiding” workshops. Stasia’s barn contains an old Vandercook, a 20th-century printing press that Woody reveres so much that he has “memorized its anatomy.” ffitch, who loves detailed terminology, luxuriates in Woody’s pleasure at just knowing “there was such thing as a half-­pica lever, a sliding knee stick, a slug cutter, a cylinder eccentric,” let alone using them. Stasia allows him access to the press, and dangles the possibility of giving it to him. In Woody’s imagination, owning it would give him a real life as an artist, which, in turn, might help him stay clean. This desire, along with his addiction itself, makes him highly susceptible to Stasia’s manipulation, even as his mother and best friend lead very different efforts to organize against her. Woody’s mother, Eloise, is Avalon’s people-pleasing librarian, a lifelong liberal activist who believes in civil discourse above all. On Stasia’s arrival, though, her commitment to this value is immediately shaken by the more forceful resistance proposed by the novel’s ragtag group of anti-fascists, which includes Woody’s childhood best friend, Leroi—a sweet, earnest mama’s boy who dreams of getting out of Avalon and becoming a vagabond. The novel’s goals include bringing its Lerois and its Eloises together, prodding them to collaborate despite their many disagreements. [ Read: A biting satire about the idealistic left ] But the novel’s deeper effort is to use political work—an “ordinary and necessary” part of life, ffitch has written —and the dissidence and quandaries it creates, to ask that each of its characters be brave in their own way. In every case, this means dealing with Stasia. For Woody, it also means reckoning with addiction, and for Eloise, recognizing that her desire to be an unjudgmental mother has led her to facilitating his drug abuse. For Eloise’s older child, Emma, who has two young sons, it means admitting something even harder. ffitch is uncommonly good at writing, tenderly but without sentimentality, about people who both adore their children and make colossal errors in raising them. Emma, especially where her 7-year-old son, Martin, is concerned, falls into this category. Of their dynamic, ffitch writes, “Emma loved Martin helplessly. Yet, just as helplessly, she wanted to hit him”—and she does. It’s only toward the end of the book that Emma admits that hitting her son isn’t a maternal instinct but rather a sign that she, herself, needs significant help. By braiding these stories, and many more, into the tale of Avalon defeating its giant, ffitch tells a layered, sophisticated story that expresses a clear, ethical point of view without hammering readers on the head. Not many novels for adults do this successfully, but in children’s literature, it is one of the standards for a great book. ffitch includes many in Avalon, Rise : Abiyoyo but also Frog and Toad , Herschel and the Hanukkah Goblins , The Dead Bird . Each of these books demands that its characters face their situation with courage; each one takes something that seems simple—burying a bird, celebrating Hanukkah, all sorts of mundane tasks in Frog and Toad —and surrounds it with not just emotional complication but also mischief, humor, and delight. So, too, with Avalon, Rise, as it demonstrates that white supremacists are unwelcome in town. What Avalon, Rise understands as well as the classics of children’s literature is that when you’re a small, fallible, confused person, everything is exciting but almost nothing is easy. What it understands as well as any great adult novel is how hard it is to get people to work together, no matter how high the stakes. In bringing these two clear yet complicated pieces of knowledge together, ffitch has written a remarkable book.

items.title: Thiam Baabel, l’humour au-delà des frontières
items.description: À 23 ans, Serigne Fallou Thiam, plus connu sous le pseudonyme de Thiam Baabel, fait progressivement sa place dans l’univers de la création de contenu. Installé aux États-Unis, ce jeune Sénégalais s’est lancé sur les plateformes numériques en 2024 avec une ambition : faire rire les internautes à travers des vidéos inspirées des scènes de la vie quotidienne. Des situations familières, des personnages reconnaissables et des comportements qui prêtent à sourire : voilà les ingrédients qui nourrissent l’univers humoristique de Thiam Baabel. À travers ses vidéos, le créateur mise sur des scènes dans lesquelles son public peut facilement se retrouver, tout en y apportant une touche de dérision. La spontanéité et l’autodérision constituent les ressorts essentiels de ses productions. Une approche qui lui permet de cultiver une proximité avec les internautes et de fédérer progressivement une communauté autour de son contenu. Mais le jeune créateur ne se cantonne pas aux sketchs courts. Il explore également des formats plus élaborés, avec des histoires davantage développées et un travail plus poussé sur le jeu d’acteur, la narration et la mise en scène. Une évolution qui témoigne de sa volonté de diversifier ses productions sans perdre l’humour qui a marqué ses débuts. À travers ses publications, Thiam Baabel cherche aussi à entretenir les échanges avec son audience. Une manière de rester proche de sa communauté tout en affinant son univers créatif. De la musique au football, des collaborations tous azimuts Pour élargir son champ d’expression, Thiam Baabel multiplie les collaborations avec des personnalités sénégalaises issues de différents horizons. Dans le milieu musical et artistique, il a notamment réalisé des contenus avec Wally Seck, Jahman X-Press, Ngaaka Blindé, Rèma et le groupe Safari. Le football occupe également une place dans son univers. Le créateur a ainsi produit des vidéos avec des joueurs de l’équipe nationale du Sénégal, dont Ismaïla Sarr, avec lequel il entretient une proximité particulière. Ces collaborations lui offrent de nouvelles possibilités créatives, diversifient ses contenus et lui permettent de faire dialoguer humour, musique et sport. Elles contribuent également à donner davantage de visibilité à ses productions auprès de publics aux centres d’intérêt variés. Malgré son installation aux États-Unis, Thiam Baabel garde le Sénégal au cœur de son univers numérique. À travers ses vidéos, il continue de s’adresser au public sénégalais, tout en poursuivant le développement de ses projets et en explorant de nouveaux formats. Son parcours illustre les opportunités qu’offrent les réseaux sociaux aux jeunes créateurs sénégalais. En abolissant les frontières géographiques, ces plateformes leur permettent de diffuser leurs productions à grande échelle, de nouer des collaborations avec des personnalités de différents milieux et de toucher un public bien au-delà du territoire national. A.N

items.title: Cyclisme burkinabè : El Hadj Tiemtoré Boukaré, dit 14, est décédé

Miles de personas reciben con entusiasmo a los Reyes en Ceuta: “Hoy toda España es caballa”
items.description: “¡Yo soy español, español, español!”, han gritado los ceutíes conforme han ido avanzando los Reyes por la Gran Vía de Ceuta en su primera visita a la ciudad autónoma . Carmen Mateo, de 54 años, llevaba esperando desde primera hora de la malan para tener un sitio en primera fila. “Quiero decirle que no se olvide del pueblo ceutí”, clamaba la mujer dos meses y medio después de la entrada masiva. Felipe VI y la reina Letizia han arrancado el paseíllo por el centro de urbe africana sobre las 12.30, tras aterrizar en helicóptero en el puerto. A esa hora, han empezado a repicar las campanas de la iglesia de África, patrona de la ciudad. Los ceutíes rugían en vítores a su paso. “¡Ceuta no se vende!“, ”¡Ceuta es España!" y “¡Hoy toda España es caballa!“, se ha escuchado sin cesar entre las miles de personas que se han apostados para recibir a los Reyes en su primera visita a Ceuta.
